body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p: The new "Comedy" in three acts, called the Fortune Hunters, is a compilation of old jokes and incidents, not at all worth repeating, in which the persons concerned are all seeking wives and husbands, and all explaining their intentions without the least liability to be mistaken. Some of them, it is true, those for instance who give the piece its title, are a little less personal in their designs; but they all think and talk alike, more or less, and the piece is little better throughout than an ill-managed double-meaning or a direct compound of grossness. There is a gay spark, who tells about "girls on the pavé,"—another who recommends himself to his mistress by confessing that he "has had his follies,"—a female fortune-hunter, who is divided between love and avarice, and makes up to every body she meets,—a male ditto, who engages to teach natural history to the ladies,—an old aunt, of a most impassioned description, her niece, a modest young lady, who interchanges soft looks with strangers in the street, and a drunken footman, who in the person of Mathews, gives as gross a specimen of his habits as can well be portrayed, and is the main support of the piece. You laugh now and then, just as you laugh in a common company of jokers,—sometimes at an odd look or gesture in the speaker, sometimes at the mere badness of the joke; but as to anything further, what can you expect from a production, which is made up of nothing but the indecency of the old comedy, and the ignorance of the new? It is said to be the work of a young man; and from what has been stated, the reader will see that it has all the marks of being so, without excepting the very worst train of ideas, into which a young mind of no great strength is too apt to be led. Instead therefore of being congratulated, he is to be pitied for having narrowly escaped damnation. A young man, who can put together dialogues of any kind, cannot be absolutely of the lowest order of understandings, and it is a pity that any body of the slightest promise should be left to repose on his inexperienced notions of what is superior and shining, and run the hazard of exchanging his future good sense and repute for the idle applause of lobby-loungers and foolish friends.

The new piece at this Theatre, Rich and Poor, is an Opera patched up, by the help of a compilation of music and songs, from Mr. Lewis's East Indian, and as little worthy of grave criticism as the one above-mentioned, though not so reprehensible in any respect. It is a poor imitation of the tattlers, and good old, home-returning uncles of the School for Scandal, with an addition of German effect in the sentimental part, and has little or nothing to boast of its own, except a scene which represents the trick of a man of fashion to get rid of two creditors, and which is amusing enough. They both happen to beset him at the same instant in his house, and he sees no means of escaping, but by telling each of them aside, after satisfying himself that they are ignorant of each other's persons, that the gentleman "whom he sees there" is Mr. Latitat his lawyer, come to pay him a large legacy"—having done this, he pretends to introduce them, and looking ambiguously at each and both, says, "this is Mr. Latitat, who will settle your claims." He then leaves them to their delighted anticipations; and after much scraping and smiling on both sides, the trick is discovered by presenting their respective bills to each other for payment. The sentimental part is carried to an outrageous pitch at the end. A daughter has offended her father by running away from India, with a man who is discovered to be married—she meets him again in England, and in spite of her having suffered a great deal of misery, and lived as virtuously as possible since the discovery, this father, while he is affecting all sorts of the pathetic on her account, will not listen to her outcries for pardon, but suffers himself to be followed about the stage with his knees clasped by her in her agony, till we long to get up and thump his wig about his head. The Manager should curtail this unnatural or at least disagreeable exhibition, which appears to exhaust even Mr. Fawcett's strong lungs, and is evidently too much for Miss Kelly, who is an actress of great sensibility, and enters into scenes of this kind with feelings that ought not to be wantonly put to their stretch.
